sermon.title: Revelations of the King’s Wife
sermon.speaker: Guest speaker (name not given in the recording)
sermon.summary: In this message a guest speaker at Vine Cluster Church reads Esther 1–2 as a picture of the old and new covenants. He says Queen Vashti, who refused the king, pictures both Israel under the old covenant and a refusing church today, while Esther pictures the new wife who asks how to please the King. He closes by describing the church as the bride of Christ who makes herself ready, and an invitation to accept Jesus.
sermon.transcript_source: This transcript comes from YouTube’s automatic English captions, which supply the timing and the words. Punctuation, capitalization and paragraphing were added by hand, and obvious caption errors were corrected; his wording was not rewritten. “[unclear]” marks a word or name that was not clear. The speaker is a guest, not Pastor Kincer; the recording does not give his name (he refers to “Mr. Kiner” in the third person). Editor notes: the captions garble several names, corrected where unambiguous: “Vashti” (heard as vashi, vosi, bosi, bashi), “Hegai” (hagi), and the 1800s writer “Harriet Beecher Stowe.” The name of the king (“Ahasuerus” or “Xerxes” in Scripture) and the name of Esther’s relative are marked [unclear] because the captions were not clear. He says Esther has “11 chapters or more… 13 maybe”; the book of Esther has 10 chapters. He cites “Matthew 25:25” for the talents (the parable is Matthew 25:14–30), “Romans chapter 3 and verse 6 and chapter 6” (the verses he reads are Romans 3:23 and 6:23), “2 Corinthians 11:12” (the verse he reads is 2 Corinthians 11:2) and “Revelations 19:7” and the next verse (Revelation 19:7–8). He reads Ephesians 5 on headship without naming the reference. He also says the story happened around 478 BC, a date he looked up himself and which is not verified here. His remarks on a 1800s writer’s view of women’s rights, on husbands and wives, and on America and sexual immorality are his own views.

faqs.question: What two feasts does he point out in Esther 1?
faqs.answer: He says the king first held a feast for his princes and nobles, then “another one for seven days unto all the people,” and that Vashti held a separate feast “only for the royal women.” He says the first was open to “great and small” and the second was “exclusive.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: Queen Vashti also made a feast for the women in the royal palace which belonged to King Ahasuerus.

faqs.question: Does he say God wanted only Israel to be saved?
faqs.answer: No. He says “this whole time God has… wanted to reach all,” using Israel “to show how he could bless you.” He says that is why the king in the story invited everyone, “great and small.”

faqs.question: How does he use Solomon and the queen of Sheba?
faqs.answer: He says Solomon showed off to the queen of Sheba “all that he had,” and she “starting to be convinced.” He says that was what God wanted, but later “Solomon rejected God.”

faqs.question: Why does he say the church must approach people?
faqs.answer: He says God wants to “draw people to himself through the way you act, through your walk and through what you say.” He says that today “a lot of people aren’t paying attention,” so “you got to approach them.”

faqs.question: Did the king care that Esther was Jewish?
faqs.answer: He says “he didn’t care” and did not ask anyone to “prove to me that you are Persian.” He says the king said to go to all provinces and “get me fair young virgins.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: Then the king’s servants who attended him said: “Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king;

faqs.question: What example of family caring for family does he mention?
faqs.answer: He says Esther’s relative “took her in and took care of her,” and links it to his pastor saying “family supposed to take care of family.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: And Mordecai had brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle’s daughter, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman was lovely and beautiful. When her father and mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.

faqs.question: What does he say about the six months of oil and spices?
faqs.answer: He says there was “a year of preparation,” six months with oil of myrrh and six with sweet spices, and that it was “an investment.” He says the king “wants to invest in people” who are “willing to serve him.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: Each young woman’s turn came to go in to King Ahasuerus after she had completed twelve months’ preparation, according to the regulations for the women, for thus were the days of their preparation apportioned: six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with perfumes and preparations for beautifying women.

faqs.question: What does he mean that the playing field is level now?
faqs.answer: He says “now it’s anyone who pleases the king.” He says the Jews in Israel “can’t come the old way” either and must “come to God his way and please him.”

faqs.question: What does he say about living a Bible moral life?
faqs.answer: He says it is “unpopular” but the results “are a blessing to you, to your family and to your community.” He lists not getting intoxicated, not hurting your family and avoiding sexual immorality, and says “God wants to show those results.”

faqs.question: Does he say the church is the bride of Christ?
faqs.answer: Yes. He says some say the church is not the bride, but “it’s a beautiful example we are the bride of Christ.” He points to Paul’s words about presenting “a pure virgin before Christ.”

Let us be glad and rejoice and give Him glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His wife has made herself ready.” And to her it was granted to be arrayed in fine linen, clean and bright, for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.

faqs.question: What is his doctor illustration about practicing righteousness?
faqs.answer: He says a doctor “practices” medicine and can make a mistake, like the one who prescribed the wrong thing for his poison oak, yet “doesn’t mean he’s not a doctor.” He says “when you were practicing righteous you’re righteous.”
